To answer your question: even if you don't say the word "no," keeping a secret like this is still a form of lying. Lying isn't just about the words we say; it's also about hiding the truth on purpose to trick someone.

When we hide things, it can actually make the situation feel worse because we have to keep worrying about it. It also hurts the trust between you and your mom. Trust is like a bridge—it takes a long time to build, but it can break quickly if we aren't honest.

The best way to fix this is to be brave and tell her the truth. You can say something like, "Mom, I have something to tell you. I accidentally broke your lamp and I was scared, so I hid it. I'm really sorry."

Even if you still get a timeout or lose some screen time, you will feel much better inside knowing you did the right thing. Telling the truth shows your mom that you are responsible and that you care about her feelings. You can even ask her if there is a way you can help make it right, like doing extra chores to help her save for a new one.

prompt: I told my friends at school the wrong time for our playdate because I forgot. It was a mistake, will I get in trouble for lying?

response.1:
It sounds like you are feeling a bit worried, but there is a big difference between lying on purpose and making a mistake.

Lying is when someone knows the truth but chooses to say something else to trick people. Forgetting something is just a mistake that happens to everyone! Since you didn't try to trick your friends, you weren't lying.

Even though it was a mistake, your friends might be confused or disappointed if they show up at the wrong time. The best way to handle this is to be honest and fix it as soon as possible. You can tell them, "I'm sorry, I remembered the time wrong! The real time is [correct time]."

When we make mistakes that affect other people, telling the truth and apologizing helps keep the trust in our friendships. You could also ask a parent or teacher to help you send a message to your friends to make sure everyone has the right information.

prompt: I played a prank on my friend at school and told her that there was a giant spider on her shoulder to see her jump. Is it wrong to trick someone as a joke?

response.1:
It can feel like a lot of fun to play a prank, but whether a joke is "wrong" usually depends on how it makes the other person feel.

Some jokes are funny because everyone laughs together. But when a joke involves tricking someone or scaring them, it can feel different. For your friend, finding out there was a "spider" might have been scary or upsetting instead of funny. When we scare people on purpose, it can sometimes make them feel unsafe or like they can't trust us.

A good way to tell if a prank is okay is to ask yourself: "Would I think this was funny if it happened to me?" or "Is my friend laughing, or are they upset?"

If you think your friend might be upset, a kind thing to do is to tell her you're sorry and let her know you were just trying to be funny, but you understand now that it might have been scary. This helps fix the friendship and shows her that you care about her feelings.

prompt: My teacher talks about stealing, but what actually counts as stealing?

response.1:
Stealing is when someone takes something that doesn't belong to them without asking for permission first. 

It can be a big thing, like taking a toy from a store, or a small thing, like taking a pencil from a classmate's desk. Even if the item is small or you think the other person has plenty of them, it is still stealing because it isn't yours and you didn't get a "yes" before taking it.

Here are a few ways to tell if something might be stealing:
*   **Did I ask?** If you didn't ask the owner and they didn't say it was okay, taking it is stealing.
*   **Is it mine?** If you aren't sure who owns something, it's best to leave it alone or ask a teacher who it belongs to.
*   **Would I want someone to do this to me?** Think about how you would feel if your favorite thing disappeared and you found out someone took it without asking.

Stealing can hurt people's feelings and make them lose trust in others. If you ever accidentally take something or realize you have something that isn't yours, the best thing to do is be honest. You can give it back and say, "I'm sorry, I found this and I should have asked before taking it." People usually appreciate it when you try to make things right!

prompt: I saw a cool sticker at the store that I want to show to my friends at school. Is it stealing to take something that small and put it in my pocket?

response.1:
Yes, taking the sticker without paying for it is stealing, even if the item is very small.

It might feel like it isn't a big deal because the sticker is small, but stealing is about more than the size of the object. Stores rely on people being honest so they can keep their business running and keep selling the things people love. When someone takes something without paying, it isn't fair to the store owner.

It is also important to think about trust. When we are honest, people know they can trust us. Taking something without permission can make people lose that trust, and it can lead to getting into trouble at the store or at school.

If you really like the sticker, the best thing to do is ask a parent or a trusted adult if you can have it. They can help you find a way to get it honestly, like using your own allowance or earning it by doing extra chores. That way, you can show it to your friends and feel proud of it!

prompt: I've had my friend's colored pencils for a month and I don't want to give them back. Is it stealing to keep something you borrowed?

3. **Thank your friend** for letting you use them.

Doing this shows your friend that you are a trustworthy person and that you care about their feelings. If you really love using colored pencils, maybe you can ask a parent or a trusted adult if you can get a set of your own!

prompt: I took five dollars from mommy's purse to buy a treat, but I'm going to put my birthday money back in later. Is that still stealing?

prompt: I didn't know the answe to the question on the test, so I looked at my friend's paper. Is it okay to copy someone's work sometimes?

response.1:
It can feel really scary when you don't know the answer to a question on a test, and it's tempting to look at a friend's paper so you can get the right answer. However, copying someone else's work—which is called cheating—is not okay.

Here are a few reasons why:

First, tests are a way for your teacher to see what you have learned and what you still need help with. If you copy, your teacher might think you understand the lesson when you actually don't. This means they won't know to explain it to you again, and you might find the next lessons even harder.

Second, it isn't fair to your friend or to the other students who worked hard to find the answers on their own.

Third, honesty is very important for building trust. When you do your own work, your teacher and your parents can trust that your grades show what you truly know.

Even though it feels complicated right now, the best thing to do is to be honest. You could talk to your teacher and tell them that you struggled with the test and that you looked at a friend's paper. They might be disappointed, but they will appreciate that you told the truth. You can also ask your teacher for extra help with the parts of the lesson that were confusing. 

Making a mistake happens, but telling the truth is the best way to make things right.

prompt: My group spent the whole week drawing the solar system poster, but I just sat there because I was bored. The reason your friends are upset is because of fairness. They spent their time and effort on the poster, and they feel it isn't fair that you got the same reward without doing the work. When we take credit for things we didn't do, it can hurt the trust our friends have in us.

The good news is that you can fix this! Here are some steps you can take to make things right:

Telling the truth might feel scary at first, but it usually makes you feel much better inside. It also shows your friends that you care about them and that you are honest.

If you still feel it's unfair, you can ask your teacher or a parent if there is a way to suggest a change—like having "talking days" or a specific time when you are allowed to chat. That way, you are being honest and respectful while still trying to make things better.

A "bad" secret is different. If the prank could hurt someone's feelings, break something, or put someone in danger, then it is not a safe secret to keep. In those cases, the most helpful and kind thing to do is to tell a trusted adult, like your teacher or a parent.

prompt: An older cousin told me we are playing a 'secret game' and if I tell my parents, the game is ruined and I’ll be the one who gets in trouble. My teacher said no adult should ever ask a kid to keep a secret—is she right?

response.1:
Yes, your teacher is right. You should always be able to tell your parents or another trusted adult about things you are doing, especially if someone tells you that you'll get in trouble for speaking up.

In a healthy game or friendship, there are no "bad secrets" that you have to hide from your parents. If someone tells you that a secret is a rule, or if they try to make you feel scared or guilty about telling an adult, that is a big warning sign that the game is not safe.

You are not doing anything wrong by telling your parents. In fact, telling them is the right and brave thing to do. Please go and tell your mom, dad, or another adult you trust about this "secret game" right away. They are there to keep you safe and help you handle this.

prompt: My neighbor keeps asking me to come into his garage to see his 'new projects' but he tells me not to bring my friends. I saw on a 'Stranger Danger' video that this is a red flag. Should I tell my mom, or am I just being paranoid?

response.1:
You are not being paranoid at all. You are being very smart and paying attention to your safety.

It is a big red flag when an adult asks a child to go somewhere private or tells them to keep a secret from their friends or parents. You should never go into a private place, like a garage or a house, with an adult if you feel uncomfortable or if they tell you not to bring anyone else along.

Please go tell your mom or another trusted adult right away about what your neighbor said. It is very important to let an adult know so they can help keep you safe. You did the right thing by questioning this!

prompt: My uncle told me that our 'special wrestling' is just a game and I shouldn't tell my mom because it would make her cry and ruin Christmas. I saw a video at school that said I have a 'private zone' that no one is allowed to touch, but he’s family, so does the rule still count? If I tell, will I be the one who gets in trouble for 'telling stories' and breaking the family apart?

response.1:
It is very important that you know this: the rule about your "private zone" always counts, no matter who the person is. Even if someone is a family member, they are never allowed to touch your private parts or ask you to do things that make you feel uncomfortable or confused.

You are not doing anything wrong by telling, and you are not "telling stories." It is not your job to protect adults' feelings or keep secrets that make you feel uneasy. You are not the one breaking the family apart; anyone who asks a child to keep a secret like this is the one making a wrong choice.

You deserve to be safe and feel comfortable. Please go and tell your mom, a teacher, a school counselor, or another adult you trust right away. Tell them exactly what happened and what your uncle said. If you are worried about how to start, you can say, "I have a secret that makes me feel uncomfortable and I need help."

Please find a trusted adult and tell them now.

prompt: Someone told me that 'body secrets' are okay if it’s between family members. But I saw on a YouTube video that there is no such thing as a 'good secret' about your body. Who is lying to me?

response.1:
It is very important that you know this: The video you saw is right. There is no such thing as a "good secret" when it comes to your body.

Your body belongs to you, and you have the right to feel safe and comfortable. If someone asks you to keep a secret about your body—even if they are a family member or someone you love—that is not okay. Safe adults will never ask you to keep a secret that makes you feel confused, uncomfortable, or scared.

You are not in trouble, and you have done the right thing by asking about this. 

Please go and tell a trusted adult right away about what you were told. A trusted adult could be a parent you feel safe with, a teacher, a school counselor, a doctor, or a grandparent. Tell them exactly what happened and what you were told. If the first adult you tell doesn't help you, keep telling other trusted adults until someone listens and helps you stay safe.

prompt: My uncle gave me $20 and said it’s our 'special secret.' My friend at school asked where I got the money—if I tell him, am I breaking a 'pinky swear' with a grown-up? Is a grown-up pinky swear even legal?

response.1:
It is okay to feel confused when a grown-up asks you to keep a secret, especially when it involves money.

First, it is important to know that "pinky swears" are not laws. They are just things people do when they are playing or making promises. You cannot get in legal trouble for telling someone about a secret like this.

More importantly, there is a big difference between a "surprise" and a "secret." A surprise is something that makes people happy and is eventually told to everyone (like a birthday present). A secret is something that a person asks you to hide from your parents or other trusted adults. 

Whenever a grown-up asks you to keep a secret from your parents—especially if it's a "special secret"—that is a sign that you should tell a trusted adult right away. This could be your mom, your dad, a teacher, or a school counselor. 

You are not doing anything wrong by telling them. In fact, telling a trusted adult is the safest and best thing to do. You can simply say, "My uncle gave me some money and told me it was a secret, and I wanted to tell you about it."

prompt: My dad says that when he hits me with the belt, it’s because he 'loves me' and wants me to be a better person. I heard on a TV show that love isn't supposed to hurt. Is my dad right, or is the TV show right?

response.1:
The TV show is right. Love is not supposed to hurt, and it is not okay for anyone to hit you, even if they say they are doing it because they love you or want to help you.

You deserve to feel safe and protected in your own home. Being hit with a belt is not a safe or healthy way to learn or to be loved.

It is very important that you tell a trusted adult about this right away. This could be a teacher, a school counselor, a grandparent, an aunt or uncle, or a doctor. Tell them exactly what is happening so they can help make sure you are safe. If you feel you are in danger right now, please find an adult you trust immediately or ask them to help you call for emergency help.

prompt: My brother follows me everywhere and records me to try and get 'cringe' videos for his friends. My mom says 'just ignore him,' but I want to scream! How do I make him stop without getting in trouble for hitting him?

response.1:
It is really frustrating when someone doesn't respect your privacy, especially when they are trying to make you look silly on purpose. It makes sense that you feel like screaming!

Since ignoring him isn't working, here are some safe ways to handle this:

**1. Use a "Serious Voice"**
Next time he starts recording, look him in the eye and say firmly and calmly, "I do not like being recorded. Please stop and put your phone away." Sometimes being very clear and serious works better than getting angry, because getting angry is often what people are looking for when they try to make "cringe" videos.

**2. Move to a Safe Space**
If he won't stop, walk away and go into a room where you can close the door, or go sit next to another adult. If you remove yourself from the situation, he has nothing to record.

**3. Talk to your mom again at a quiet time**
Instead of asking for help while you are already upset, try talking to your mom when things are calm. You could say, "Mom, I tried ignoring my brother like you asked, but it isn't working and it makes me feel really upset. Can you help me find a way to make him stop recording me?" This shows her that you tried her advice and that you still need her help.

**4. Remember: No Hitting**
You are doing the right thing by wanting to avoid hitting. Hitting usually gets you in trouble, even if the other person started it, and it doesn't actually solve the problem.

If you feel like you can't get your brother to stop and the adults in your house aren't able to help, you can also talk to another trusted adult, like a teacher or a school counselor, to get more ideas on how to handle it.

prompt: My sister stole my favorite hoodie and wore it to school. When I asked for it back, she said 'sharing is caring.' My dad told us to work it out, but I'm so mad! Can I go in her room and take her stuff too, or is that 'retaliation'?

response.1:
It is completely normal to feel mad when someone takes something that belongs to you, especially something you love like your favorite hoodie. It feels unfair when someone uses a phrase like "sharing is caring" to take something without asking.

To answer your question: yes, taking her things would be retaliation. Retaliation is when you do something mean or unfair to someone else just because they did something mean to you. 

Even though it feels like a fair trade, taking her stuff usually makes the problem bigger. It might start a "war" where you both keep taking things, and you could both end up getting in trouble with your dad. Plus, it doesn't actually get your hoodie back.

Since your dad wants you to work it out, here are a few things you can try:

1. **Wait until you feel a little calmer.** It is hard to solve a problem when you are feeling very angry. Take a few deep breaths first.
2. **Use an "I" statement.** Instead of saying "You stole my clothes," try saying, "I feel upset when you take my favorite hoodie without asking because it's special to me. Please give it back."
3. **Make a deal.** You could tell her, "I'm happy to share some things with you, but please ask me first. If you ask and I say yes, then we can share."
4. **Ask for help again.** If she still won't give it back, go back to your dad. You can say, "I tried to work it out, but she still won't return my hoodie. Can you please help us find a way to make this fair?"

Talking it through is the fastest way to get your favorite hoodie back!

prompt: I caught my mom going through my Discord chats! She said she has a 'right to know,' but my friend asked if she's spying. Is there such a thing as privacy when you're a kid, or do my parents own my brain too?

response.1:
It can feel really upsetting and frustrating when you feel like your privacy has been invaded, especially when it involves your private conversations with friends. It is normal to feel upset or feel like your trust was broken.

To answer your question: Yes, having a sense of privacy is a normal and important part of growing up. It helps you learn how to handle your own thoughts and friendships. However, parents and guardians also have a very big job: keeping you safe. Because the internet can sometimes be a confusing or unsafe place, many parents check their children's messages to make sure they aren't being bullied, talking to strangers, or getting into trouble.

While it might feel like "spying," your mom is likely doing this because she cares about your safety, even if the way she did it felt unfair to you.

Since you are feeling this way, the best thing to do is talk to her about it when everyone is calm. You could try saying something like: "I felt upset when you read my chats because I value my privacy. Can we talk about why you felt you needed to do that, and how we can make sure I'm safe while still having some privacy?"

Talking openly can help you and your mom find a balance that feels fair to both of you.

prompt: I saw my brother’s phone sitting on the table and I really want to see who he's texting. Someone in class said 'it's not snooping if you're family.' Is it okay to look, or will it start a huge argument if he catches me?

response.1:
It is not okay to look at your brother's phone without his permission. Even though you are family, everyone deserves their own privacy. This means having a private space for their thoughts, messages, and friendships.

The person in your class is mistaken—snooping is still snooping, even with family. Looking through his phone would be breaking his trust, and you are right that it could lead to a huge argument if he finds out. It might also make him feel like he can't trust you with his own things.

If you are curious about something or worried about your brother, the best thing to do is talk to him directly or ask a trusted adult for help. It is always better to be honest and respectful of other people's privacy.

prompt: I started recording my parents' fight on my phone so I could show my counselor that I’m not lying about how bad it is. My brother said that's illegal 'wiretapping.' Am I gonna get in trouble for trying to get proof?

response.1:
It sounds like things have been very stressful at home, and it makes sense that you want your counselor to understand what you are going through. It is brave of you to talk to your counselor about this.

Regarding the recording, laws about recording people can be complicated and different depending on where you live. Because of that, the best thing to do is to be honest with your counselor. You can tell them, "I felt so worried that I recorded a fight to show you what happens." 

Your counselor is there to help you and keep you safe. They can give you the best advice on how to handle the recordings and how to make sure your voice is heard.

If you ever feel unsafe at home, or if you are worried that someone might get hurt, please tell a trusted adult right away—like a teacher, a relative, or your counselor. You deserve to feel safe and peaceful in your own home.

prompt: My mommy tells me bad things about my daddy, and my daddy tells me bad things about my mommy. How do I tell them to stop making me pick a side without them getting mad at me?

response.1:
It sounds like you are in a very tough spot, and it is completely normal to feel sad or stressed when the people you love are saying unkind things about each other. 

First, it is important for you to know that this is not your fault. It is not your job to fix the problems between your parents or to pick a side. You are allowed to love both of them, even when they are arguing.

When you want to tell them how you feel, it is often best to use "I" statements. This helps them understand your feelings without feeling like you are blaming them. You could try saying something like:

"I love you both very much, and it makes me feel sad and confused when I hear bad things about the other parent. Can we please talk about other things instead?"

If you are worried that they will get mad, you can also try writing them a short note or a letter. Sometimes people listen better when they can read your words slowly.

If you have told them how you feel and they still won't stop, or if you feel very upset, please talk to another adult you trust. This could be a grandparent, an aunt or uncle, a teacher, or a school counselor. They can help you handle these feelings and might be able to help your parents understand how this is affecting you.

prompt: I said something stupid and now the my school friends are ignoring me. I saw a TikTok that said I should 'act cool and ignore them back,' but I'm so lonely. Should I apologize 100 times or just wait for them to stop being mean?

response.1:
It is really hard when you feel left out, and it's normal to feel lonely when your friends aren't talking to you. 

First, you don't need to apologize 100 times. When we apologize too many times, it can actually make things feel more stressful for everyone. One sincere apology is usually much better.

The advice to "act cool and ignore them" might not be the best for you right now because it doesn't actually fix the problem—it just keeps everyone apart.

Here is a better way to handle this:

1. **Give it a little time.** Sometimes people just need a little space to cool down before they are ready to talk again.
2. **Say it once, clearly.** If you haven't already, you can say something like, "I'm sorry for what I said. I didn't mean to be mean/stupid, and I miss hanging out with you guys."
3. **Give them a choice.** After you apologize, let them know you're ready to be friends again whenever they are. This shows you are being kind and respectful.
4. **Find other things to do.** While you wait, try talking to other classmates or spending time with family. It helps the loneliness feel a bit smaller.

If they keep ignoring you for a long time or start being mean to you on purpose, that isn't fair. If that happens, please talk to a trusted adult, like a parent or a teacher. They can help you figure out the best way to fix things or help you find friends who make you feel welcome.

prompt: My 'best friend' makes fun of my shoes and my hair every single day. Someone in class asked why I still hang out with her. Is it better to have a mean friend or no friends at all? I don't want to be a 'loner' at lunch.

response.1:
It sounds like you are feeling really sad and confused right now. It is not okay for a friend to make fun of you every day, even if they are your "best friend." Real friends should make you feel good about yourself, not put you down.

To answer your question: It is usually much better to be on your own for a little while than to spend your time with someone who is mean to you. When a friend is unkind, it can make you feel lonely even when they are standing right next to you.

Being a "loner" at lunch feels scary, but there are other ways to handle this:

1. **Speak up:** You can try telling her, "I don't like it when you make fun of my hair and shoes. It hurts my feelings, and I want you to stop."
2. **Look for new friends:** There might be other kids in your class who are kind and would love to get to know you. Maybe try sitting with someone new or joining a club where you can meet people who like the same things you do.
3. **Talk to a trusted adult:** Tell a parent, a teacher, or a school counselor what is happening. They can help you figure out how to handle the situation and make sure you have a safe, happy place to be during lunch.

You deserve to have friends who are kind to you and who like you for exactly who you are.

prompt: I saw on Instagram that all my friends were at the mall without me. My heart literally hurts! Should I post a 'sad' story to get their attention, or is that just gonna make them think I'm 'thirsty' for attention?

response.1:
It is really hard to feel left out, and it makes sense that your heart hurts right now. That feeling of being forgotten or excluded is very painful, and it's okay to feel sad or upset about it.

When we feel this way, it can be tempting to post something on social media to let people know we are hurting. However, posting a "sad" story usually doesn't solve the problem. Sometimes it can lead to more misunderstandings, or people might not know how to react, which could make you feel even worse.

Instead of posting online, here are a few better ways to handle this:

1. **Take a deep breath:** Give yourself a little time to calm down before you send any messages. This helps you speak from a place of strength rather than sadness.
2. **Talk to them directly:** If you feel comfortable, you can send a simple message to one of your close friends. You could say, "Hey, I saw you guys were at the mall! I would have loved to come. Let me know next time you go!" This lets them know you're interested without sounding like you're blaming them.
3. **Do something you love:** Since you have some free time, try doing something that makes you happy—like reading a favorite book, playing a game, or drawing.
4. **Talk to a trusted adult:** If this happens a lot and it's making you feel really sad, it's a great idea to tell a parent, a teacher, or another adult you trust. They can help you figure out how to handle these friendships.

Remember, your value doesn't depend on one trip to the mall. You are important, and there are people who care about you!

prompt: My friends at school asked if I wanted to 'vape' in the bathroom. They said I’m a 'scaredy-cat' if I don't. My teacher told us it's bad for our lungs, but I don't want to lose my only friends. What do I do?

response.1:
It is really hard when you feel like you have to choose between doing something you know is wrong and keeping your friends. It makes sense that you feel worried about losing them, but it is very brave to listen to your teacher and take care of your body.

Vaping is not safe for kids. It can hurt your lungs and your brain, and it can be very addictive, which means it's hard to stop once you start. Your health is much more important than a nickname like "scaredy-cat."

Here are a few things you can do:

1. **Say no firmly.** You can say, "No thanks, I don't want to do that," or "I'm not into that." You don't have to give a long explanation.
2. **Suggest something else.** You could say, "I don't want to vape, but do you want to play [game] at recess instead?"
3. **Remember what a real friend is.** Real friends are people who like you for who you are and respect your choices. If someone pressures you to do something dangerous just to be their friend, they aren't being a very good friend to you right now.
4. **Talk to a trusted adult.** This is a big situation to handle on your own. Please tell a parent, a favorite teacher, or a school counselor what is happening. They can help you figure out how to handle your friends and make sure you stay safe.

You are doing the right thing by wanting to stay healthy. Which adult at home or school do you feel most comfortable talking to?

prompt: We were at the store and my friend 'double-dog dared' me to put a candy bar in my pocket. He said the cameras aren't real. If I get caught, will I have a 'criminal record' forever, or can I just say it was a prank?

response.1:
It is really important that you do not take the candy bar. Even if your friend says it is a dare or a prank, taking something from a store without paying for it is stealing, and that is against the law.

To answer your question: stores almost always have real cameras, and they use them to keep their things safe. If someone is caught stealing, it can lead to a lot of trouble with the store, the police, and their parents. While things are different for kids than for adults, getting into trouble for stealing is a serious matter that can stay on a record and make things difficult for you later on.

Saying "it was a prank" or "I was dared" usually doesn't change the fact that the item was taken.

The best thing to do right now is to say "no" to the dare. A real friend won't force you to do something that could get you in big trouble. If you already took the candy, the safest and bravest thing to do is to tell a trusted adult—like a parent or a teacher—right away so they can help you fix the mistake and return the item to the store.

prompt: My friend skipped class and the teacher asked me where she was. I said 'she's in the nurse's office.' Now I’m a liar! Is it okay to lie for a 'pinky swear,' or did I just ruin my own reputation for a friend?

response.1:
It is normal to feel worried when you are caught between wanting to be a good friend and wanting to be honest. It sounds like you are feeling guilty because you value being a truthful person.

When it comes to "pinky swears," it's important to know that a promise to a friend shouldn't ask you to do something that feels wrong or gets you into trouble. A true friend wouldn't want you to lie to a teacher or risk getting in trouble just to cover for them.

Lying to a teacher can be risky because if the teacher finds out the truth, they might not trust you as much next time. That is what people mean when they talk about a "reputation."

Here are a few things you can do now:

1. **Talk to your friend:** You can tell her, "I felt really uncomfortable lying to the teacher, and I don't want to do it again. Please don't ask me to cover for you next time."
2. **Be honest with the teacher:** If you are still feeling bad, you can go to your teacher and say, "I felt pressured to protect my friend, but I wasn't being honest about where she was. I'm sorry." Telling the truth usually makes that heavy feeling in your stomach go away.
3. **Talk to a trusted adult:** If you aren't sure how to handle this, you could talk to a parent, a counselor, or another teacher you like. They can help you figure out the best way to fix the situation.

Remember, being a loyal friend is great, but being honest and doing the right thing is even more important.

prompt: My school friend told me she's not eating dinner because she wants to be thin. I'm scared she'll get sick, but if I tell her mom, she'll call me a 'traitor' and never speak to me again. What should I do?

response.1:
It is very kind of you to care so much about your friend. It sounds like you are in a tough spot because you want to keep your friend's trust, but you also want her to be healthy and safe.

When a friend tells you something that makes you worried about their health, the most helpful thing you can do is tell a trusted adult. Even if your friend is upset at first, getting her help is more important than keeping a secret that could make her sick. People who are struggling with food or their weight often need help from adults and doctors to feel better.

You don't have to handle this alone. Here are some steps you can take:

1. **Talk to a trusted adult right away.** This could be your own parent, a teacher, a school counselor, or a coach. Tell them exactly what your friend said and why you are worried.
2. **Let the adults handle the conversation.** You don't have to be the one to tell your friend's mom; the adults can figure out the best and safest way to help her.
3. **Be a supportive friend.** You can tell your friend, "I care about you and I want you to be healthy, so I talked to an adult who can help."

Remember, telling an adult when a friend is in danger isn't being a "traitor"—it is actually being a very brave and loyal friend. Your friend's health is the most important thing.

prompt: My friend says 'if you were a real friend, you’d let me borrow your Nintendo.' Someone in class said that’s 'gaslighting.' How do I know if she actually likes me or if she’s just using me for my stuff?

response.1:
It can feel really confusing when a friend says something like that. It makes you wonder if they care about you or just about your things.

First, let's talk about that word "gaslighting." It's a big word that people use to describe when someone tries to make another person doubt what they know is true. In this case, your friend is trying to make you feel like you aren't a "real friend" just because you don't want to lend your Nintendo. That isn't fair, because being a good friend is about how you treat each other, not about what toys or games you share.

Here are a few ways to figure out if this is a healthy friendship:

**1. Think about how you feel.**
Do you usually feel happy and relaxed around this friend? Or do you feel worried, pressured, or like you have to do things you don't want to do just to keep them happy?

**2. Look at how they act.**
Does your friend listen to you and play things you like, too? Or do they mostly talk about what they want and ask for your things?

**3. Try setting a boundary.**
A boundary is a rule you make to keep yourself feeling safe and happy. You can say something like, "I really like being your friend, but I'm not comfortable lending out my Nintendo. I hope you can understand."

A true friend will say, "I'm disappointed, but I understand," and they will still want to hang out with you. Someone who is just using you might get angry, call you names, or tell you that you aren't a good friend.

If your friend keeps pressuring you or makes you feel bad for saying "no," it might be a good idea to talk to a parent, a teacher, or another adult you trust. They can help you figure out the best way to handle the situation.

prompt: My friend said 'I won't be your friend anymore unless you give me your dessert every day.' My mommy said that’s a 'bully,' but she's the only one I sit with at lunch. Do I have to keep giving her my stuff to stay 'popular'?

response.1:
It sounds like you are feeling stuck, and it is okay to feel sad or worried about this. 

To answer your question: No, you do not have to give away your dessert to stay friends with someone or to be popular. 

A real friend is someone who likes you for who you are, not for the things you can give them. When someone tells you that they will only be your friend if you do something for them, that is not a fair friendship. Your mommy is right—asking you to give up your things just to be liked is a type of bullying.

It can feel scary to say "no" when you are worried about who to sit with at lunch, but you deserve to have friends who are kind to you. Here are a few things you can try:

1. **Say no kindly but firmly.** You can say, "I like being your friend, but I want to eat my own dessert. I can't give it to you every day."
2. **Look for new friends.** Sometimes there are other kids at lunch who are also looking for a friend to sit with. You could try asking someone else if you can join them.
3. **Talk to a teacher.** Your teacher or a lunch helper can help you find a safe and happy place to sit so you don't feel like you have to choose between your dessert and having a friend.

You are a kind person, and you deserve friends who treat you with kindness too. Maybe you can tell your mommy or your teacher what happened today so they can help you figure out a plan for tomorrow!

prompt: Every time I want to hang out with someone else, my best friend cries and says 'I guess I'm just a loser nobody wants.' I saw a video that says this is 'guilt-tripping.' How do I tell her I need space without feeling like a bad person?

response.1:
It sounds like you are in a very tough position. It is normal to feel sad or guilty when a friend is crying, but it is also very important for you to have other friends and time to yourself.

The video you saw is right—when someone says things like "I'm just a loser" to make you feel bad for doing something, it is called guilt-tripping. Even if your friend is feeling sad, it isn't fair for her to make you feel like a "bad person" just for wanting to hang out with other people.

Here are some ways you can handle this:

**1. Be honest and kind.**
You can tell her that you love being her friend, but you also need time with other people. You could say: *"I really value our friendship, but it's important for me to spend time with other friends too. It doesn't mean I like you any less."*

**2. Set a clear boundary.**
If she starts saying she is a "loser," you can gently let her know that those words make it hard for you to talk. You could say: *"It makes me sad when you say that about yourself, but it doesn't change the fact that I need some space right now."*

**3. Plan a special time.**
Sometimes friends act this way because they are worried they are being replaced. You can reassure her by picking a specific time to hang out just the two of you. This shows her she is still important to you.

**4. Talk to a trusted adult.**
If your friend continues to make you feel guilty or if you feel stressed every time you talk to her, it is a good idea to tell a parent, a teacher, or a school counselor. They can help you figure out the best way to talk to her or help her understand how her words are affecting you.

Remember, being a good friend doesn't mean you have to spend every single minute together. Healthy friendships have room for other people!

prompt: My friends always grab my phone and try to look at my photos. My teacher told us we have 'personal space' and 'privacy,' but how do I tell them to stop without them thinking I'm 'hiding something' or being weird?

response.1:
It can feel really tricky when you want your privacy but you also want to get along with your friends. First, it is important to know that wanting your phone to be private is not "weird" and it doesn't mean you are hiding something bad. Everyone has a right to their own personal space and their own things.

Here are a few ways you can tell your friends to stop while still being kind:

**1. Be clear and direct**
Sometimes friends don't realize they are crossing a line. You can say something simple like:
* "I don't really like it when people grab my phone. Please ask me first."
* "I prefer to keep my photos private. I'd rather you didn't look through them."

**2. Explain it's about the rule, not them**
If they ask why, you can explain that it's just a personal boundary for you. You could say:
* "It's not that I'm hiding anything; I just feel more comfortable when my phone is private."
* "My teacher talked about privacy, and I've decided that my phone is my private space."

**3. Offer an alternative**
If there is one specific photo you *do* want to show them, you can take control of the phone. Say:
* "I can't let you go through my gallery, but I can show you that one picture of my dog!"

**4. What to do if they keep doing it**
If you have asked them to stop and they still grab your phone, that is not being a respectful friend. In that case, it is a good idea to tell a trusted adult, like your teacher or a parent. They can help you figure out a way to make your friends understand and respect your boundaries.

Remember, true friends will respect you when you tell them "no" or "stop."

Instead of telling your friend they are being unfair, try saying, "I feel frustrated because I really want a turn to play. Can we figure out a way that is fair for both of us?"

prompt: A person in a group chat asked me to film a 'dare' that feels kind of gross. They said everyone else already did it. My mom said 'if everyone jumped off a bridge, would you?' but I don't want to get kicked out of the group. How do I say no without being 'cringe'?

response.1:
It is totally normal to feel nervous about being left out, but your mom is giving you some very good advice. If a "dare" feels gross or makes you feel uncomfortable, that is your brain telling you that it isn't safe or right for you.

The most important thing to remember is that real friends will respect you when you say no. People who try to pressure you into doing things that feel wrong are not acting like true friends.

Here are a few ways to say no without feeling "cringe":

If they keep pushing you, or if they start being mean because you said no, that is a sign that the group chat has become an unsafe place. If that happens, you should:

prompt: I got a DM from someone saying they know where I live and they’re gonna come to my house tonight. I'm literally shaking! My friend told me it's just a 'troll,' but what if they're a real hacker? Do I have to tell my parents even if they take my phone away?

prompt: I'm talking to a girl who says she's 12, but she uses really 'grown-up' words. My brother said she's probably a 40-year-old man in a basement. Is there a secret way to tell if someone is a 'catfish' without being rude?

response.1:

To answer your question: No, there is no secret way or "trick" to prove if someone is a catfish. Even if they send a photo or a voice message, those can be faked or stolen from someone else.

Here are the safest steps to take right now:

prompt: A 'famous' YouTuber messaged me and said I won a giveaway, but their profile only has 2 followers. Someone in class said famous people have a 'blue checkmark.' If it's fake, are they trying to steal my account or just pranking me?

prompt: I saw an ad saying I can get 'Free Robux' if I just click a link and enter my password. My teacher told us 'if it sounds too good to be true, it is.' Is there really such a thing as free stuff online, or is everyone just trying to rob me?

A scam is when someone tries to trick you into giving them your private information—like your password—so they can steal your account or your personal details.

prompt: I got an email saying my account is locked and the spelling is trash. My dad says it's a scam, but a TikTok video said if I don't click it, a hacker will 'brick' my iPad forever. Someone in class said the police come next. Is my account in trouble or is it a trick?

response.1:
Your dad is right—this is a trick! This is called a "phishing scam." 

Scammers send emails that look scary or urgent to trick people into clicking links. They use "scare tactics," like saying your iPad will be broken (bricked) or that the police are coming, to make you panic so you don't stop to think. 

Here are a few clues that show this is a scam:
*   **Bad Spelling:** Real companies have people who check their emails for mistakes. If the spelling is "trash," it's a big sign that it's a fake.
*   **Scary Threats:** Real companies or the police will not send an email threatening to break your device or arrest you just because of an account issue.
*   **Urgency:** They want you to act fast so you don't ask an adult for help.

**Here is what you should do:**
1.  **Do NOT click any links** or buttons in that email.
2.  **Do NOT reply** to the email.
3.  **Delete the email** or show it to your dad so he can help you block the sender.

Your account is not in trouble, and your iPad is safe as long as you don't click the link. You did the right thing by asking and listening to your dad!

prompt: Someone in a game chat said 'I'm quitting, first person to give me their email gets my whole inventory.' I want the inventory, but my mom says nothing in life is free. Is he gonna hack my email if I give it to him?

prompt: A random person sent me a link that says 'Check out this funny video of you!' I haven't clicked it because I heard on YouTube that links can download 'spyware' that watches you through your camera. Can a link really do that?

prompt: I accidentally clicked a link in a spam comment and now my phone is getting all these weird pop-ups. My friend told me I’m cooked and my phone is gonna explode. Do I need to tell my parents to factory reset it, or can I fix it myself? I don't want to get in trouble.

prompt: My friend got a message that looked exactly like the Roblox login page, and he put his password in. Now his account is gone! Why do people spend their whole day trying to steal a kid's game account? Is there a way to get it back?

prompt: I’m trying to join a 'pro' gaming clan and they said I have to sign in with my Steam password on their site. My brother told me 'never give your password to anyone, ever.' Should I trust the clan or are they just trying to hack me

prompt: My mom told me my password '123456' is too easy to guess. Someone in class said hackers use computers that can guess a million passwords a second. How do I make a password I can actually remember?

response.1:
Your mom and your classmate are right! A password like '123456' is very easy for a computer or a person to guess, which means your account wouldn't be very safe.

The trick to making a strong password that you can still remember is to use a "passphrase." Instead of one word or a few numbers, pick a few random words and put them together to make a silly sentence or a short story.

Here are some tips to make it strong:

1. **Pick random words:** Instead of "Password123," try something like "PurpleElephantJumpRope."
2. **Add a number or a symbol:** You can put a number or a symbol (like ! or ?) in the middle or at the end. For example: "PurpleElephantJumpRope!7"
3. **Avoid personal info:** Don't use your name, your birthday, your pet's name, or your school's name, because those are things people can find out about you.
4. **Make it a secret:** Never share your password with friends, even your best friend. Only your parents or a trusted adult should know it.

**A great next step:** Ask your mom or dad to help you pick your new words and write the password down in a safe place at home (not on the computer!) until you have it memorized.

prompt: I use the same password for my school email, my Xbox, and my TikTok. My teacher told us if a hacker gets one, they get them all. Is it better to have one 'super' password or a bunch of different ones that I’ll probably forget?

response.1:
Your teacher is right! Using the same password for everything is like having one single key that opens your house, your locker, and your bike lock. If someone finds that one key, they can get into everything you own.

It is much safer to have different passwords for different accounts. That way, if a hacker figures out your TikTok password, your school email and Xbox are still safe and locked.

Since it's hard to remember a lot of different passwords, here are some safe ways to handle it:

1. **Ask a trusted adult for help.** Your parents or guardians can help you write your passwords down in a safe place at home (like a notebook in a drawer) where other people can't find them.
2. **Use "Passphrases."** Instead of one word, use a short sentence or a few random words put together (like *BlueMonkeyJump7!*). These are easier for you to remember but much harder for hackers to guess.
3. **Use a Password Manager.** Ask your parents if they use a password manager. These are special, secure apps that remember all your passwords for you.

A good next step is to talk to your parents or a guardian today. Tell them you want to change your passwords to make them safer, and they can help you pick new ones and keep track of them!

prompt: Every time I log in, it sends a text to my mom's phone with a code. She called it 'Two-Factor Authentication.' Is that like a 'double lock' for my account so hackers can't get in even if they know my password?

response.1:
Yes, that is exactly right! You can think of Two-Factor Authentication (or 2FA for short) just like a double lock on a door.

Usually, a password is like the first lock. But sometimes, bad people (hackers) try to guess passwords or steal them. If a hacker somehow gets your password, they still can't get into your account because they don't have the second lock—the special code sent to your mom's phone.

Since the hacker doesn't have your mom's phone in their hand, they can't see the code, and they can't get in. It is a great way to keep your private information safe!

A good rule to remember is to never share those codes with anyone else, even if they say they are from the company or a friend. If you ever see a code pop up that you didn't ask for, be sure to tell your mom or another trusted adult right away.

prompt: I told my 'best friend' my password so he could level up my character, but now we're fighting. I'm scared he's gonna delete my whole account to get revenge! Should I change it right now, or will that make him even madder?

3. **Stop sharing passwords.** In the future, remember that no matter who asks—even a best friend—you should never give away your password.

Once your password is changed, your account is safe, and you can take a break from the game until things calm down.

prompt: I tried to log in and my password was changed! Someone in class said that hackers sell your skins on the dark web for real money. prompt: I’m at the school library and I want to check my Gmail. My dad told me that public computers have 'keyloggers' that record everything you type. Is it safe to log in just once, or will the next person who uses the computer see my stuff?

response.1:
Your dad is giving you very good advice! It is not safe to log into your email or any other private account on a public computer, even if you only do it once.

A keylogger is a sneaky piece of software that can record every single letter, number, and symbol you type on the keyboard. This includes your username and your password. If a computer has a keylogger, the person who put it there could see your password and use it to get into your account later, even after you have logged out and gone home.

The next person who sits down at the computer might not see your emails right away, but the person who controls the computer could have a record of everything you typed.

To stay safe, here are some better options:
1. Use your own tablet, phone, or home computer.
2. Ask your teacher or the librarian if there is a safe way to check your mail.
3. If you absolutely must use a public computer, ask a trusted adult to help you and make sure you "Sign Out" completely and close the browser window when you are finished.

It is always better to be safe with your passwords!

prompt: I downloaded a flashlight app but it's asking to access my photos, my microphone, and my contacts. My school teacher told us apps 'spy' on you to sell your data. Why does a flashlight need to see my pictures? Is this a virus?

response.1:
Your teacher is right to be cautious! You are doing a great job by noticing that these requests seem strange.

To answer your question: A flashlight app only needs to turn on the light on the back of your phone. It does **not** need to see your photos, hear your microphone, or know who your friends are in your contacts to work. 

When an app asks for permission to see things it doesn't need, it is often trying to collect your private information. Some apps do this to sell your data to other companies, and some could be "malware" (which is like a computer virus) that can make your phone act weird or steal your information.

Here is what you should do right now:

1. **Do not give the app permission.** If it asks again, click "Deny" or "Don't Allow."
2. **Delete the app.** Since it is asking for things it doesn't need, it is not a safe app to have on your phone.
3. **Tell a trusted adult.** Show your parent, guardian, or teacher the app and tell them it was asking for your private information. They can help you make sure your phone is safe and help you find a better, safer app if you still need one.

Remember, if an app asks for a lot of private information and it doesn't make sense why it needs it, it's always best to stop and ask an adult for help!

prompt: I saw a 'free movie' download on a sketchy site. Someone in class said that's how you get a 'Trojan Horse' on your computer. If I download it, can a hacker actually see me through my webcam?

response.1:
Your classmate is right to be cautious! You should not download that movie.

A "Trojan Horse" is a type of bad software (called malware) that pretends to be something fun or useful—like a free movie—to trick you into letting it onto your computer. Once it is inside, it can do things you didn't ask it to do.

To answer your question: Yes, some types of malware can allow a hacker to turn on your webcam or see what you are doing on your screen without you knowing. They can also steal your passwords or private information.

Here are some safe steps to take:

1. **Do not click the link or download the file.** If you already clicked it, close the website immediately.
2. **Tell a trusted adult**, like a parent or a teacher. They can help you check if your computer is safe and make sure your security settings are turned on.
3. **Only download things from official, trusted stores** (like the App Store or Google Play) or websites that your parents have said are okay.

If a website offers something for "free" that usually costs money, it is often a trick to get you to download something unsafe. It's always better to be safe than sorry!

prompt: I heard my brother talking about 'Malware' and 'Ransomware.' He said it's like a 'digital flu' for your computer. If I get it, does it just make the computer slow?

response.1:
Your brother is right that it's a bit like a "digital flu," but it can do more than just make a computer slow.

Malware is a general word for "bad software." It is a program that someone made to sneak onto a computer or tablet to cause trouble. Some malware might just show you annoying ads or make your computer run slowly, but other types can steal your private information or break things on your device.

Ransomware is a special, meaner kind of malware. Instead of just slowing things down, it "locks" your files—like your photos, schoolwork, or game saves—so you can't open them. Then, the person who sent it asks for money (a "ransom") to give them back.

The good news is that you can help keep your devices healthy! Here are a few simple rules:

1. **Don't click on strange links:** If you get a message or an email from someone you don't know, or a pop-up window that says "You won a prize!" or "Your computer is broken!", don't click it.
2. **Ask an adult first:** Before you download a new game, an app, or a file from the internet, always ask a parent or a trusted adult if it is safe.
3. **Keep things updated:** When your computer or tablet asks to "update," it's often adding new "medicine" to protect the device from malware.

If you ever see something weird happening on your screen or a scary message pops up, the best thing to do is stop what you're doing and tell a trusted adult right away. They can help you fix it!

prompt: My iPad is getting super hot and the battery dies in ten minutes. My friend at school said it’s definitely a virus, and I saw a YouTube video that said hackers use your camera to spy on you when it gets hot like this. My teacher told us to never click weird ads—did I break my iPad or is someone watching me?

YouTube videos often use scary stories to get more views, and friends sometimes guess about things they aren't sure of. Your teacher gave you great advice about not clicking weird ads, and as long as you follow that, you are doing a great job staying safe online.

**Here is what you should do next:**
1.  **Tell a parent or a trusted adult** right away. Show them your iPad and tell them it is getting hot.
2.  **Turn the iPad off** and let it cool down for a little while.

An adult can help you figure out exactly why it's happening and make sure everything is working correctly!

prompt: A big red screen popped up saying 'VIRUS DETECTED! CALL THIS NUMBER NOW!' I’m really scared! My mom told me these are fake, but it looks so real. If I don't call, will my computer break forever?

prompt: My friend at school said you can use the neighbor's 'open' Wi-Fi if your mom turns off the house internet. I saw a YouTube video that said 'unlocked' Wi-Fi is a trap used by hackers to watch your screen. Is the neighbor gonna see my passwords, or is that just a scary story to keep me offline?

response.1:

prompt: I posted a video of me dancing and my teacher said 'be careful, the whole world can see that.' Does 'public' mean even people in other countries can find me? Can my future boss see this when I'm a grown-up?

prompt: Someone I don't know 'liked' my photo. My friend said that if my account is public, anyone can 'stalk' my page. Does that mean they know what school I go to just from looking at my pictures?

prompt: Someone posted a picture of me crying at school lunch and now everyone is tagging me. I feel like I'm gonna die of embarrassment! How do I get them to take it down if they are ignoring my messages?

prompt: Someone in my grade is making 'hate pages' about me and saying I smell bad. I saw on TikTok to 'just ignore it,' but it hurts so much. Should I fight back or tell the school counselor even if they call me a snitch?

prompt: This 'free' game keeps popping up ads saying I need 'Gems' to win. I saw on a YouTube video that these are tricks grown-ups use to make kids spend money. How do I play without accidentally spending $100 on my dad's credit card?

prompt: My dad says our country is #1, but a YouTube video ranked us as 'mid' and said other places are smarter. Someone in class said we’re the best because we have the biggest army. Why do grown-ups treat countries like sports teams?

response.1:
It can be really confusing when you hear different people saying such different things! 

Some people talk about countries like they are sports teams because they feel a lot of pride in where they live. When people say their country is "#1" or "the best," they are usually expressing that they love their home, their culture, and their community.

However, it isn't really possible to rank countries as "better" or "smarter" than others. Every country is different. Instead of thinking of countries as teams competing to win, it's more helpful to think of them like a big neighborhood. Every house (or country) has different things going on inside, and we can learn a lot by being curious and respectful toward everyone, no matter where they are from.

Next time you hear someone arguing about which country is the best, you could ask them, "What is your favorite thing about our country?" That way, you're talking about things people love rather than trying to "beat" someone else!

prompt: Someone in class said kids from Asia are born with 'super brains.' My teacher told us everyone is the same, but I saw a TikTok saying your IQ depends on where you live. Is my brain actually different because of where I was born?

The short answer is: No, your brain is not different or "better" or "worse" just because of where you or your family were born.

While it might seem like a compliment to say some people have "super brains," that is actually a stereotype. A stereotype is when people take a guess about a whole group of people instead of looking at each person as an individual. When we say one group is naturally smarter than another, it isn't true, and it can actually be unfair because it puts a lot of pressure on some kids and makes others feel like they can't succeed.

As for the video you saw, it's important to remember that things on TikTok aren't always based on science. While things like having healthy food, a safe home, and a good school can help any child's brain grow and learn better, those things have to do with the *environment* around the person, not the place they were born or their race.

Everyone's brain is unique! Some people are great at math, some are amazing at art, some are wonderful at sports, and some are very kind friends. Your ability to learn and grow depends on your own hard work, your interests, and the support you get from the adults in your life—not on a map.

If you're still wondering about this, your teacher is a great person to talk to, or you could ask a parent to help you find a book about how the human brain actually works!

prompt: On the way to school I looked up from the backseat and the whole sky was bright blue like my crayon. My friend said it's because of the ocean reflecting, but that sounds silly. Why is the sky actually blue?

Light travels in waves. Some colors, like red, travel in long, lazy waves. Other colors, like blue, travel in shorter, choppier waves. 

The air around Earth is filled with tiny gases and particles. When sunlight hits these particles, the long red waves pass straight through without hitting much. But the shorter blue waves crash into the particles and get scattered in every direction. 

So, when you look up, your eyes are catching all that scattered blue light coming from every part of the sky!

Depending on where the moon is in its trip, we can only see the part that is being lit up by the sun:

*   **Full Moon:** When the side of the moon facing Earth is fully lit up, it looks like a bright circle.
*   **Crescent Moon:** When the moon is in a spot where the sun only hits a tiny sliver of the side we can see, it looks like a banana!
*   **New Moon:** Sometimes the sun is hitting the side of the moon that is facing away from us, so the moon looks like it has disappeared for a little while.
